course.title: ML Hybrid Course
course.lead: One ordered path through the books already on this laptop, split into day-sized lessons. Each day pulls the author's own words from a named page range, then points at a local exercise. You never re-open a book from page one: the day tells you the exact pages, and the recall block re-tests what you already completed. From Day 17 the same rhythm carries an AGI track: Togelius on what generality even means, the OpenCog architecture survey, context engineering, agentic coding, and a closing gate on governance as architecture.
course.method: Kumon-style rhythm, borrowed from the local developer path: **recall** (5 min, from memory) → **read the author** (10–15 min, one bite) → **practice** (20–30 min, one local exercise) → **check** (5 min, run it and log the correction). Move on only when you can explain the idea without looking. Review days re-test earlier days at 1, 3, 7 and 21 lessons back, automatically.
course.teacher_basis: Structure grafted from the local SyncSenta teacher curriculum (`Sync-0.0.2/data/ai_curriculum.json`): every sub-strand carries learning outcomes, prerequisites, expected misconceptions and assessment evidence. Those four fields are what the days below use as `idea`, `recall`, `misconception` and `check`. Not KICD/CBC-aligned; a personal adaptation.

days.title: What machine learning actually is
days.idea: Machine learning is a program whose behaviour is shaped by data instead of by hand-written rules; the test of it is performance on unseen examples.
days.recall: From memory, define machine learning in one sentence and give one example where you would NOT use it. If you cannot say the sentence, this day is a repeat day, not a reading day.
days.misconception: Believing a model is intelligent because it produced an output. An output is a prediction, not a truth.
days.practice: Open `../ml-exercises/README.md` and read the pathway list only. Then write, in your log, which of the 12 local exercises maps to each idea you expect to meet in this course. No code today.
days.check: Say the definition out loud without the page open, then write one sentence on why unseen data matters. Both must exist in your log before marking complete.
days.gate: Explain the difference between a rule-based program and a learned program using a non-tech example of your own.

days.title: Supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement: the categories
days.idea: The three families differ by what the learning signal is: labelled answers, unlabelled structure, or reward after acting.
days.misconception: Calling anything 'AI' that is only if-else logic. Name the learning signal or it is not a category.
days.practice: Take three apps you use daily (M-Pesa alerts, YouTube, SMS) and classify the learning signal in each. Write it down; this is the skill the recall blocks will re-test.
days.check: Re-test Day 1 from memory before reading. If it faded, redo Day 1's gate first.
days.gate: Give one worked example per category without looking, and say what the model would be wrong about in each.

days.title: The ML toolbox: models as tools, not identities
days.idea: A toolbox of model families (regression, trees, clustering, nets) chosen by the shape of data and the decision needed.
days.practice: Do `../ml-exercises/exercises/00_fundamentals/01_split_data.py` (stdlib, offline). The point is train/test separation before any model exists.
days.check: Run `python3 ../ml-exercises/run_tests.py` and read every line it prints, pass or fail.
days.gate: Pick a tool for a problem you define yourself, and defend the pick against one alternative.

days.title: Data scrubbing and setting up your data
days.idea: Most of the work is making the data trustworthy: missing values, duplicates, wrong units, leakage.
days.misconception: Cleaning after fitting. Anything computed from the whole dataset before the split leaks the test set into training.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/00_fundamentals/02_standardize.py`. Then deliberately corrupt one row and re-run to watch the failure.
days.check: Day 3 recall (1 back) plus: name three leakage routes you have personally caused.
days.gate: Clean a small messy CSV of your own and record each choice with a reason.

days.title: Data engineering, the way production does it
days.idea: Training data is a pipeline with owners, schemas and versions, not a folder of files.
days.practice: Sketch a data pipeline for one SyncSenta-style dataset on paper: source, transform, store, validate, serve. Mark where it breaks.
days.check: Compare your sketch against the extracted text and name one stage you invented that the author warns about.
days.gate: Explain schema drift to a non-engineer in three sentences.

days.title: Regression analysis: fitting a line you can defend
days.idea: Regression estimates a relationship; the fit quality is a claim about data, not a promise about the world.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/01_models/04_fit_line.py` then `../ml-exercises/exercises/00_fundamentals/03_regression_metrics.py`.
days.check: Day 5 recall (1 back) and Day 2 recall (3 back).
days.gate: Report one metric in your own words, then say what it hides.

days.title: Error metrics and validation sets that mean something
days.idea: MAE, MSE and hold-out validation answer different questions; choose the metric from the cost of being wrong.
days.misconception: Chasing accuracy on an imbalanced problem. 99% accuracy can be a useless model.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/01_models/05_confusion_counts.py`. Predict the numbers before running, then compare.
days.check: Day 6 recall (1 back), Day 4 (3 back), Day 1 (back to the definition).
days.gate: For a loan-approval problem, name the metric you would defend in a review and why.

days.title: Bias and variance — plus a hard review of Days 1–7
days.idea: Underfitting misses structure; overfitting memorises noise. Complexity trades one error for the other.
days.practice: No new exercise. Re-solve `01_split_data.py` and `03_regression_metrics.py` from a blank file, closed solutions. Log every mistake.
days.check: Write the one-sentence idea of Days 1–7 from memory first; only then open the pages. Faded days get re-added to your queue.
days.gate: 90% of the recall prompts answered cold. If not, repeat this day tomorrow instead of advancing.

days.title: Decision trees and ensemble modelling
days.idea: Trees split on features to make decisions explainable; bagging and boosting buy accuracy by averaging or correcting many trees.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/02_unsupervised/07_assign_centroid.py` is adjacent practice in nearest-neighbour thinking; then hand-draw a tree for a daily decision.
days.check: Day 8 (1 back), Day 6 (3 back), Day 2 (7 back).
days.gate: Explain why many weak learners beat one strong learner, with an analogy you would use with a student.

days.title: Artificial neural networks without the mysticism
days.idea: A network is weighted arithmetic plus a non-linearity, tuned by gradient descent; layers compose features.
days.misconception: Thinking depth alone equals understanding. Depth is capacity, not comprehension.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/01_models/06_gradient_step.py`. Predict the next weight before running.
days.check: Day 9 (1 back), Day 7 (3 back), Day 3 (7 back).
days.gate: Walk one gradient step by hand on paper with numbers you choose.

days.title: Logistic regression, properly (interview depth)
days.idea: Logistic regression is a linear score squashed into a probability; the decision threshold is a business choice.
days.practice: Re-derive the sigmoid from the page without looking, then code it in the style of `../ml-exercises/exercises/01_models/05_confusion_counts.py`.
days.check: Day 10 (1 back), Day 8 (3 back), Day 4 (7 back).
days.gate: Answer two interview questions from this chapter in writing, closed book.

days.title: Information theory: entropy as surprise
days.idea: Entropy measures average surprise; cross-entropy is the loss you pay when your predicted distribution differs from reality.
days.practice: Compute entropy by hand for a two-outcome event at p=0.5, 0.9, 0.1. Then compute it in Python from scratch, no libraries.
days.check: Day 11 (1 back), Day 9 (3 back), Day 5 (7 back).
days.gate: Explain why cross-entropy punishes confident wrong answers harder than loss functions you already know.

days.title: How large language models actually work
days.idea: An LLM predicts the next token from context; training is expensive, inference is a search over probabilities.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/03_language_models/09_chunk_text.py`. Everything here is local strings, no API calls.
days.check: Day 12 (1 back), Day 10 (3 back), Day 6 (7 back), Day 1 (21 back — the definition again).
days.gate: Explain a hallucination using only next-token prediction, no hand-waving.

days.title: Retrieval: chunking, embedding, ranking
days.idea: Retrieval grounds generation in documents you chose; chunk quality and ranking decide what the model gets to see.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/03_language_models/10_rank_documents.py` plus `08_cosine_similarity.py`.
days.check: Day 13 (1 back), Day 11 (3 back), Day 7 (7 back), Day 2 (21 back).
days.gate: Given a wrong answer from a RAG setup, list the three places the fault could live.

days.title: Why machine learning systems fail
days.idea: Failures are usually pipeline, data and feedback-loop failures, not model-quality failures.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/04_responsible_ai/12_group_rates.py`. Note which group metric moves and why that matters.
days.check: Day 14 (1 back), Day 12 (3 back), Day 8 (7 back — review day again), Day 3 (21 back).
days.gate: Write a one-page post-mortem for a system that got silently worse, naming the monitoring you would have needed.

days.title: Build and optimise one model end to end
days.idea: You own the whole loop now: split, clean, fit, measure, explain, improve.
days.practice: Write a single stdlib Python program that loads a small CSV you choose, splits it, fits the line from Day 6, and reports metrics from Day 7. No pandas. Then re-run `../ml-exercises/run_tests.py` and keep it green.
days.check: Cold-write the one-sentence idea of Days 1–15. Anything you cannot write goes back into your queue as its own day.
days.gate: Present the model in five minutes to an imaginary colleague, including one thing you would change with more data.

days.title: Why nobody agrees on what AGI means
days.idea: AGI is a contested term, not a milestone. Togelius opens by saying the definitions conflict; the useful move is to ask general at *what*, and to treat intelligence as a measured capacity to do many tasks rather than a substance a system either has or lacks.
days.recall: Day 16 (1 back), Day 14 (3 back), Day 10 (7 back). From memory: name one thing your Day 10 neural network cannot do that a Day 14 retrieval system can, and say which of the two is more general.
days.misconception: Treating AGI as a finish line a lab crosses on a Tuesday. A single threshold cannot be measured across tasks of different difficulty, so any claim of we reached AGI is a claim about the benchmark, not the machine.
days.practice: Open `../ml-exercises/exercises/00_fundamentals/01_split_data.py` and its solution. Everything you say about generality must be tested on data the model has not seen - that is the whole reason the train/test split exists. Then write the sentence: my generality claim will be tested on ___.
days.check: Say the definition of AGI the book works with, without the page, and give one example where that definition would classify a spreadsheet as intelligent.
days.gate: Explain to a friend why passing the test is weak evidence of generality, using a test you have personally taken.

days.title: A brief history of superhuman narrow machines
days.idea: Machines have beaten humans at one celebrated skill after another - checkers, chess, Go, image recognition, quiz games - and each win turned out to be narrow. The pattern is that every milestone quietly needed more human-built scaffolding than the publicity admitted.
days.recall: Day 17 (1 back), Day 15 (3 back), Day 11 (7 back). Name three superhuman narrow systems and, for each, the one human decision that made its victory possible.
days.misconception: Believing a win at a game proves general ability. It proves the machine can search a well-defined state space with a hand-written evaluation function, which is a different claim entirely.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/01_models/05_confusion_counts.py` - implement it, then look at what the exercise makes you count. Write one paragraph: what would Deep Blue's confusion matrix look like, and what would it have no rows for?
days.check: Say why a benchmark can be saturated by narrow methods, and name the benchmark your own field treats as if it were generality.
days.gate: Given a system that beats every human at task T, list three things it still cannot do, and say which of the three a recruiter would care about.

days.title: Intelligence (natural): the measurement before the machine
days.idea: Human intelligence was made scientific by psychometrics: many cognitive tests correlate, and that correlation - the g factor - is a statistical observation, not a discovered organ. AGI debates inherit this measurement problem wholesale.
days.recall: Day 18 (1 back), Day 16 (3 back), Day 12 (7 back). Define the g factor in one sentence and say what it is a correlation between.
days.misconception: Reifying the score. IQ names a pattern in test results; treating it as a fixed quantity inside a head is the error, and the same error waits for anyone who reduces a model to one benchmark number.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/03_language_models/10_rank_documents.py` then `11_parse_model_json.py` - both are about ranking and scoring outputs. Run them, then write the sentence a score ranks, it does not explain, and name one place in this course where you have been tempted to forget it.
days.check: Explain in one sentence why factor analysis finds structure in data rather than in people.
days.gate: Argue both sides for ninety seconds each: g is real, and g is an artefact of how the tests are built. Then say which side a measurement designer should assume.

days.title: Intelligence (artificial): how to score a machine fairly
days.idea: If intelligence is measured performance across many task environments, the hard part is the task distribution: normalise by difficulty, weight breadth over peak, and refuse to average a chess engine with a spam filter.
days.recall: Day 19 (1 back), Day 17 (3 back), Day 13 (7 back). State the definition of artificial intelligence this book measures against, then name the two things it forces you to specify.
days.misconception: Comparing systems on one task and calling the winner more intelligent. That is a claim about the task; a fair comparison says what fraction of the task space was covered.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/00_fundamentals/03_regression_metrics.py` is the seed of this day. Reuse its idea: write a rubric that scores three different tiny programs on breadth, not only accuracy. Write the rubric before you pick the programs.
days.check: Say how you would normalise two benchmarks of different difficulty, out loud, without notes.
days.gate: Design a 10-task test that would separate a calculator from a language model, and say which of your ten tasks is doing the most work.

days.title: Varieties of AGI: the taxonomy that ends most arguments
days.idea: AGI collapses several independent properties: breadth, robustness, autonomy, and generality of learning. Once you separate the axes you can stop arguing about the label - a system can be strong on one axis and absent on another, which is why two people can both be right about the same model.
days.recall: Day 20 (1 back), Day 19 (3 back), Day 14 (7 back). Name the axes the taxonomy separates, then place one system you used this month on each.
days.misconception: Reading AGI as one dial from weak to strong. It is a set of dials, and marketing flattens them on purpose because a single dial makes a better headline.
days.practice: Score four systems you already have on this laptop - the models from `../ml-exercises/`, a retrieval pipeline, a code agent, and a spreadsheet macro - on breadth, robustness and autonomy, 1 to 5, in your log. That table is the deliverable.
days.check: Say which axis your own work genuinely improves, and which one you have been implying it improves.
days.gate: Someone says this model is nearly AGI. Ask the two questions that make the sentence precise, then answer them for a system of your choice.

days.title: Practical AGI development: what you would build this week
days.idea: Building toward generality now means engineering transfer between tasks: shared representations, world models that predict, and architectures where learning one thing does not erase another. It is a programme of components, not one magic algorithm.
days.recall: Day 21 (1 back), Day 20 (3 back), Day 15 (7 back). Name the three component families and say which one Day 5's data-debt discussion already told you how to fail at.
days.misconception: Believing scale alone delivers the components. More compute buys the same behaviour faster; it does not buy a world model and it does not protect an old skill from being overwritten.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/02_unsupervised/08_cosine_similarity.py` - shared representations are this day's claim made concrete. Implement it, then compare the vectors of two tasks you care about and write down what similar would actually mean for transfer between them.
days.check: Explain catastrophic forgetting in one sentence and say which of your own pipelines is most exposed to it.
days.gate: Sketch, in six lines, the smallest system that learns task B without losing task A. Name the part that would actually break.

days.title: Self-supervised learning of foundation models
days.idea: Foundation models work because prediction without labels is nearly free: mask a span, predict it, and the gradient arrives from the corpus itself. That is the bridge from the supervised world of Day 6 to the LLM world of Days 13-14, and it explains both the reach and the brittleness.
days.recall: Day 22 (1 back), Day 21 (3 back), Day 13 (9 back - it is the LLM day). Say what the label is in self-supervised learning and where it comes from.
days.misconception: Thinking self-supervised means unsupervised in the Day 7 clustering sense. There is still a target and still a loss; the trick is that the target is generated from the input instead of by an annotator.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/03_language_models/09_chunk_text.py` then `11_parse_model_json.py`. Chunk a document, then predict what a masked model would have to infer about your own writing. Record the one chunk boundary that changed meaning.
days.check: Explain next-token prediction versus masking, and say which one makes retrieval augmentation necessary.
days.gate: A stakeholder says we will fine-tune our own foundation model. List the three questions that decide whether that is reasonable, and the answer that would stop you.

days.title: Open-ended learning in virtual worlds
days.idea: Games and simulated worlds let a system be tested on tasks nobody wrote for it: co-evolve an agent with its environment and you get a curriculum that never runs out. Quality-diversity beats a single best score, because the interesting result is a range of working strategies.
days.recall: Day 23 (1 back), Day 22 (3 back), Day 16 (8 back). Define quality-diversity in one sentence and contrast it with the single-number ranking you wrote about on Day 19.
days.misconception: Assuming simulated results transfer. A world model built by a game engine still differs from the messy physical and social world, and the gap is exactly where the failures land.
days.practice: `../ml-exercises/exercises/01_models/06_gradient_step.py` is the smallest possible agent learning from feedback. Run it, then write the local version of this day's idea: a fitness function plus one thing that must vary, not merely improve.
days.check: Say why an environment that cannot get harder teaches nothing, and name the exercise in this course whose difficulty is fixed by its test suite.
days.gate: Design an open-ended curriculum for a skill you are learning that is not coding. Name the agent, the environment, and what counts as a novel task.

days.title: Consciousness, superintelligence, and what any of it owes you
days.idea: Three separate questions get fused in public debate: whether a machine is conscious (untestable, with no agreed theory), whether it will be much better than us at everything (a distribution claim, not a switch), and who governs the consequences (an institutional claim). Mixing them produces confident nonsense in both directions.
days.recall: Day 24 (1 back), Day 23 (3 back), Day 18 (7 back). Separate the three questions in one sentence each, without the page.
days.misconception: Reasoning about machine suffering or machine supremacy from human intuition, which was built for other humans and for tools, and is unreliable for both of these.
days.practice: Write the paragraph you would actually send a decision-maker: what is genuinely uncertain about AGI, what is merely contested, and what is already decided by systems you have run. Then read `../security-exercises/exercises/03_response/08_incident_checklist.py` and steal its discipline - name the owner and the trigger, not the mood.
days.check: Name one AGI claim you have repeated that you cannot now support, and say what evidence would change your mind.
days.gate: Argue the cautious position and the dismissive position for two minutes each, then say which one you would bet your work on and why.

days.title: Cognitive architectures: the survey that predates the hype
days.idea: Before foundation models, people built whole minds on paper and in code - SOAR, ACT-R, Cyc and the rest - by deciding what memory is, what a goal is, and how a decision gets made. The value of the survey is vocabulary: architecture is what you choose when the model is not enough.
days.recall: Day 25 (1 back), Day 24 (3 back), Day 22 (4 back), Day 19 (7 back). Name two architectures from the survey and the one thing each insists a mind must have.
days.misconception: Assuming the field started with transformers. Working memory, an episodic store, planning over a world model - all of it was engineered and argued about decades ago, badly, on the record.
days.practice: Take the three component families you listed on Day 22 and match each to a named mechanism in this chapter. Where the chapter's mechanism is stronger than your plan, change your plan and log the change.
days.check: Say what a cognitive architecture provides that a model checkpoint does not.
days.gate: Explain to your Day 1 self why a chatbot plus memory is still not an architecture, and name the missing piece by its old name.

days.title: From prompts to context: engineering what the agent is shown
days.idea: Context engineering is deciding what an agent sees and when: the semantic blueprint, the chaining of steps, the validation loop. It replaces write a cleverer prompt with design the information flow, which is why it behaves like software engineering and not like magic.
days.recall: Day 26 (1 back), Day 25 (3 back), Day 23 (4 back), Day 20 (7 back). Define context in one sentence, then say what Day 23's token-prediction limit has to do with it.
days.misconception: Believing a bigger context window removes the problem. More room to put things is not a plan for what belongs there, and a full window degrades quietly rather than failing loudly.
days.practice: Build the smallest real version: take one unsolved exercise from `../ml-exercises/exercises/01_models/` and write a context file an agent would need to solve it - task, allowed tools, two worked examples, and the validation check. Then attempt it yourself using only that file and log what you had left out.
days.check: Name the three parts of your context file the agent could not have inferred, and the one it could.
days.gate: Debug this: the agent answers well on the sample and badly in production. Give the three context-related causes you would rule out first, in order, and say which is most likely.

days.title: Agentic coding: a teammate who still needs review
days.idea: Agentic coding means delegating a task, not a keystroke: the system decomposes it, touches the environment, and produces work that must be reviewed like any other contribution. The skill moves to specification, review and rollback - the parts an agent cannot own.
days.recall: Day 27 (1 back), Day 26 (3 back), Day 24 (4 back), Day 21 (7 back). Say what an agent may decide and what stays yours, as two lists.
days.misconception: Believing autonomy removes review, or that a passing test suite proves good design. Agents optimise for the check you wrote, and a weak check is worse than none because it feels like safety.
days.practice: No service needed: pick one exercise from `../ml-exercises/exercises/01_models/` you have not solved, write its specification as if handing it to a teammate (constraints, tests, forbidden changes), then solve it yourself and diff your thinking against the spec. The gap is the review skill you just practised.
days.check: Name three things you will never delegate on this laptop, and why each is cheap for you and expensive for an agent.
days.gate: Write the two-sentence policy you would give a team adopting agentic coding tomorrow, including who is accountable when it breaks production.

days.title: Trust and governance as architecture: the closing gate
days.idea: Governance is not a document bolted on after deployment; it is a property of the design - who can act, what is provable, what gets logged, and what happens when the operator is wrong. This short paper argues the architecture has to carry the trust the humans will not grant.
days.recall: Day 28 (1 back), Day 27 (3 back), Day 25 (4 back), Day 22 (7 back), Day 8 (21 back). From memory: name the one component you would refuse to ship without an audit trail.
days.misconception: Treating governance as compliance theatre. If nothing changes when a control is violated, it is a policy paragraph, not an architectural property.
days.practice: Write the capstone page: (a) the system you would build with what you have now, (b) the three failure modes from Days 21, 25 and 28 that apply to it, (c) the architectural control that answers each, and (d) the evidence a stranger could check. Then run `python3 ../ml-exercises/run_tests.py` and `python3 ../security-exercises/run_tests.py` and log both outputs - finishing the course means the code you wrote still passes.
days.check: Say, without notes, the difference between a control and a policy. Your page must contain at least two of the former.
days.gate: Defend the capstone to three critics in turn: a Day 1 beginner, a Day 21 taxonomist, and a regulator. Where you cannot answer, that is next week's study, not this course's gap.
